h(x)=xp(x), g′(θ)<0 on [0,1), g(1)=0.  On the two-point lattice

C(θ,1)−C(θ,0)=Δ(θ)=(1−θ)p(1)F(θ)=p(1)g(θ)≥0,
Δ(1)=0, Δ(θ)>0 for θ<1.

g is the product of two decreasing positive functions, hence
θ2>θ1 ⇒ g(θ2)<g(θ1) and Δ is strictly decreasing in θ on [0,1).
Hence the incremental expected penalty of moving from the lenient
corner x=0 to the strict corner x=1 falls with truthfulness,

sign[Δ(θ′)−Δ(θ)] = sign[g(θ′)−g(θ)]<0 , θ′>θ .

For θ<1 h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1) so that for every interior type
C(θ,0)=t(θ)<t(θ)+g(θ)p(1)=C(θ,1) and the unique cost minimiser is
x*(θ)≡0 on [0,1).  At the top g(1)=0 ⇒ C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1) and the
truthful type is indifferent.  In decreasing-differences notation

C(θ′,x′)−C(θ′,x)−[C(θ,x′)−C(θ,x)] = [g(θ′)−g(θ)][h(x′)−h(x)]≤0
for θ′>θ, x′>x, i.e. C has decreasing differences in (θ,x).  Hence
with the usual monotone comparative statics the best response is
weakly increasing in θ: a higher θ makes the strict auditor relatively
cheaper, Δ′(θ)<0.  In particular no interior type strictly moves to a
more lenient auditor when θ rises.  The best response is flat at the
lenient corner on the interior and the only change of preference is the
degenerate indifference at the boundary θ=1.

Strictly speaking the set
{θ: x*(θ′) < x*(θ) for θ′<θ } is empty; up to the trivial boundary
indifference the lenient auditor is strictly optimal for every
θ∈[0,1) and the (weak) preference for leniency is g(θ)>0 ⇔ θ<1.
In the binary {0,1} support this is the malpractice type θ=0 strictly
preferring x=0 and the truthful type θ=1 indifferent.  The sign of
h′(x)=p(x)+xp′(x) is the only source of ambiguity in the continuum
formulation; with the two-point technology h(1)>h(0) is guaranteed and
the conventional sorting is x* weakly increasing in θ, the opposite of
the “bad drives out good’’ story.  Colleagues 1,3,4,6,7,8 reach this
constant-pooling conclusion, while colleagues 2 and 5 state the
monotonicity with the opposite sign, a confusion of the direction of
the monotone comparative static. ∎
reflection_text.2:
The relevant $x$-dependent part of expected cost is up to the $x$-free $t(\theta)$

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)
           =t(\theta)+h(\theta)\,xp(x), \qquad 
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,$$

with $h(1)=0$. $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so $h$ is strictly
decreasing on $[0,1)$ and $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$
wherever the derivative exists. For the two point lattice

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta), 
\;p_{1}=p(1)>0,$$

$$ \Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =p_{1}h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p_{1}F(\theta)\ge0, $$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $0\le\theta<1$.
Hence $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ on the whole interior and

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1),$$

i.e. up to the irrelevant $t(\theta)$ the (weak) minimiser is
$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$ and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate.
The gain from leniency $\Delta(\theta)=p_{1}h(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$ because $h$ is decreasing.  In particular
$C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=h'(\theta)xp(x)<0$ so $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta ,x)$. With $xp(x)$ increasing in $x$ the cost
difference is monotone decreasing in truthfulness: the incentive to
avoid the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ gets weaker as $\theta$ rises.

Hence in the interior the ranking of the two audits is $\theta$-independent
up to the decreasing scale $h(\theta)$: every non-perfect type strictly
prefers the lenient auditor and the truthful type $\theta=1$ is
indifferent. In the strict monotone sense $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ never
occurs on $(0,1)$; the best response is flat $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$,
the usual weak comparative static being $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$, not decreasing. On the canonical binary support
$\{0,1\}$ this is the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring
$x=0$ and the truthful type $\theta=1$ indifferent, i.e. the strict
monotone move to a more lenient auditor is vacuous/empty and the weak
preference for leniency is the whole interior $\theta<1$, often phrased
as the empty strict set with the trivial indifference at $\theta=1$.
The sign of $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not pinned down by $p$ decreasing
alone; the usual textbook statement that a higher $\theta$ makes a
strict auditor relatively cheaper is the decreasing-differences
case $C_{\theta x}<0$. The disagreement in the round is exactly this
sign convention: the cost of strictness is decreasing in $\theta$ so a
more truthful firm is weakly more willing to bear strictness, i.e. the
sorting is towards stricter audits with truthfulness. ∎
reflection_text.1:
The expected cost up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ is
$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ and on the refusal event
${\mathbb P}\{$RS audit$\}=x(1-\theta)p(x)$.
Put $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, $h(1)=0$, $h$ strictly decreasing
because $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing, and $h(x)=xp(x)$.
Then up to $t(\theta)$
$\tilde C(\theta,x)=h(\theta) h(x)$ with $h(\theta)>0$ decreasing in $\theta$.

For the binary technology $x\in\{0,1\}$

$h(0)=0$, $h(1)=p(1)>0$,

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$.
Hence $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $0\le\theta<1$ and
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The lenient auditor $x^{*}=0$ is the unique strict
minimiser on the interior and the truthful type is indifferent.

Decreasing differences hold:
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x=
p(x)\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0$ on the support,
i.e. $C_{\theta x}<0$ because $h'(\theta)<0$.  With Topkis $x^{*}(\theta)$
is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The incremental cost of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$, so the gain from
leniency $C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)$ falls with truthfulness and vanishes
only at $\theta=1$.

Hence on the interior the choice is flat $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$, and the
usual single-crossing sorting is the opposite of the statement: a higher
$\theta$ makes a strict auditor relatively cheaper.  In the strict
monotone sense $x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$ for $\theta'>\theta$ never
occurs; the strict monotone set is empty.  In weak terms the (constant)
preference for leniency holds for all $\theta<1$, i.e. for the
malpractice type $\theta=0$ in the two-point support $\{0,1\}$, with the
trivial indifference $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$.  The $p$ decreasing alone does
not guarantee $xp(x)$ decreasing; the binary case makes the optimum
degenerate to the lenient corner.  No interior $\theta$ induces a strict
move to a more lenient auditor as truthfulness rises.
reflection_text.8:
The cost that matters for the choice of $x$ is the expected extra payment over the $x$–free tax $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta),\qquad 
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta)\,x p(x)
$$

with $h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$, $h(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$
and $F$ are decreasing so $h$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ in the monotone sense.
Up to the additive $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta)\equiv C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =p(1)h(\theta)\ge0 ,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every $\theta<1$.  Hence on the
binary lattice

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+p(1)h(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),\qquad 
0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The lenient corner $x=0$ is the unique strict
minimiser for every interior type and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate.
Formally

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

so the choice is pooled on the lenient auditor on the whole interior.
The gain from leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is
strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishes only at $h(1)=0$; the
incentive to avoid the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ is therefore
monotone decreasing in truthfulness.

In decreasing–differences notation $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)h_{2}(x)$,
$h_{2}(x)=xp(x)$.  On $\{0,1\}$ $h_{2}(0)=0<h_{2}(1)=p(1)>0$, i.e.
$h_{2}$ is increasing, $h'<0$, so $C_{\theta x}=h'(\theta)h_{2}'(x)<0$
and $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$.  The usual
single-crossing sign is therefore

$$
{\rm sign}\,C_{\theta x}=-{\rm sign}\,h_{2}'(x),
$$

and with the binary technology $h_{2}'(x)>0$.  In textbook monotone
comparative statics this is the familiar $x^{*}$ weakly increasing in
$\theta$ statement: the cost of moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$,
$\Delta(\theta)$, falls with $\theta$, so a higher truthfulness makes a
strict auditor relatively cheaper.  Because $h_{2}(x)$ is increasing the
strict preference is always for the lenient corner, so the monotone
prediction is vacuous on the interior: $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ for
$\theta<1$ and the only change in preference is the degenerate
indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.

Hence there is no interior type at which a strict increase in $\theta$
is associated with a strict move to a strictly smaller $x$.  In the strict
monotone sense the set is empty; up to the trivial indifference at the
top the weak preference for leniency holds for every $\theta<1$ and on
the two point support the only strict preference for $x=0$ is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$, the truthful type $\theta=1$ being the
indifference point.  This is the opposite of the “more truthful → more
lenient’’ intuition: truthfulness weakens the gain from leniency and the
formal comparative static is $x^{*}$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, with
pooling on $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  The disagreement in the round is
exactly the tension between the formal decreasing-differences sign and
the corner solution $h_{2}(0)=0<h_{2}(1)$ which makes the optimal
auditor flat on the interior.
reflection_text.6:
The relevant part of the expected cost is up to an $x$-free term $t(\theta)$

$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)x p(x)$

with $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ on $[0,1)$ and $h(1)=0$.
$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so $h$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$,
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever differentiable.
For the binary technology $x\in\{0,1\}$

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$, $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$

$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)\ge0$, 
$\Delta(1)=0$, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.

Hence $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every interior type and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.
Up to the irrelevant additive $t(\theta)$ the lenient corner strictly dominates
on $0\le\theta<1$ and $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with indifference only
at $\theta=1$.  The gain from leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$ because $h$ is decreasing.

In the usual monotone comparative statics language
$\partial C/\partial x =h(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ and
$\partial^{2}C/\partial\theta\partial x =h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$.
Since $h'<0$, $C$ has decreasing differences iff $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e.
$xp(x)$ increasing in $x$. On the two point lattice $0\cdot p(0)=0<1\cdot p(1)$
so the discrete incremental cost of strictness is decreasing in $\theta$.
Hence the (weak) optimal $x^{*}$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$: a higher
$\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper. This is the opposite of
“more truthful $\Rightarrow$ more lenient”.

Strict monotone movement to a more lenient auditor as $\theta$ rises never
occurs in the interior. The strict preference set for leniency is
$\{\theta<1\}$, with the unique cost minimiser $x^{*}=0$ for all $\theta<1$,
and the only non-trivial change is the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$. In the stated discrete support $\{0,1\}$ this is the malpractice
type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$ and the truthful type $\theta=1$
indifferent. The strict monotone set $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty; the weak
pooling set is $[0,1)$.

Unresolved/nuance: the sign of $p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not pinned down by $p$ decreasing
alone in the continuum. Differentiability is not assumed, so the implicit
function theorem cannot be invoked. Colleagues disagree on phrasing “$x^{*}$
decreasing vs increasing”; the disagreement is the sign convention for
decreasing differences. The economically relevant content is $h$ decreasing,
so the cost disadvantage of strictness falls with truthfulness and the
model predicts pooling on the lenient auditor for all imperfectly truthful
types, with indifference at the top.
reflection_text.4:
The relevant $x$–dependent part of expected payment is, up to the $x$–free term $t(\theta)$,

$C(\theta ,x)-t(\theta)= {\rm Prob}\{no\;report\}\;p(x)F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$

and with the normalisation $g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$,
$h(x):=xp(x)$

$\tilde C(\theta ,x)=g(\theta)h(x)$.

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so $g$ is strictly decreasing on
$[0,1)$ with $g(1)=0$, $g(\theta_{2})<g(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.
On the two point technology

$h(0)=0$, $h(1)=p(1)>0$,

so that

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)\ge 0$,

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$, and $\Delta$ is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$ in the monotone sense

$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0$ for
$\theta'>\theta$.

Hence $C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)$ for every $\theta<1$ and
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$, i.e. up to the trivial indifference at the top the
lenient corner $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$. The (weak) minimiser is

$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate,

so the model pools on the lenient auditor on the interior. The gain from
leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness, the incentive to avoid the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$
weakens as $\theta$ rises.

In the interior notation $C_{\theta x}=g'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ with
$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$. Hence

${\rm sign}\,C_{\theta x}=-{\rm sign}\,[p(x)+xp'(x)]$.

Decreasing differences $C_{\theta x}<0$, i.e. $x^{*}$ weakly increasing
in $\theta$, holds iff $p(x)+xp'(x)>0\iff h'(x)>0$. The stated
monotonicities of $p$ alone do not identify the sign of $h$, and the
implicit function theorem cannot be invoked because $t,p,F$ are only
monotone. With the binary support the sign is irrelevant: $h(0)<h(1)$
implies $\tilde C(\theta ,1)>\tilde C(\theta ,0)$ for every $g(\theta)>0$,
so the optimal choice is flat on $[0,1)$.

In particular there is no interior type at which a strictly larger
$\theta$ induces a strictly smaller $x$. Strict monotone demand for
more leniency $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is vacuous on the interior; the usual
single-crossing monotonicity is the opposite, the cost of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$ and the best response is weakly
increasing, constant $0$ on $[0,1)$ with the conventional indifference
point $\theta=1$. Weakly, the lenient auditor is preferred for every
$\theta<1$, and on the canonical two-type support this is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$ with the truthful
type $\theta=1$ indifferent. The strict monotone set for a genuine
move to a more lenient auditor as truthfulness rises is empty; up to the
trivial indifference at the top the weak preference set is $\theta<1$,
i.e. $\theta=0$ in the $\{0,1\}$ specification. This is the source of the
disagreement in the round between the “weakly decreasing $x^{*}$’’ reading
and the conventional decreasing-differences/ $x^{*}$ weakly increasing
reading.

1.text:
With the $x$ free part of the payment written as

$$ \tilde C(\theta ,x)=g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta ):=(1-\theta)F(\theta ),\qquad h(x):=xp(x), $$

up to the $x$–free $t(\theta )$ the firm minimises $g(\theta)h(x)$.
$F$ and $1-\theta$ are decreasing so that

$$g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad 
g(1)=0,\;g(\theta)>0\;\;0\le\theta<1,$$

and $g$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$.  Hence

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x), $$

so that
$C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ iff $h'(x)>0$.
For the two point technology

$$h(0)=0,\qquad h(1)=p(1)>0, $$

so that on $\{0,1\}$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)
 =g(\theta)p(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0, $$

$$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0, $$
and $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$,

$$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .$$

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1, $$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The incremental cost of moving from the
lenient corner $x=0$ to the strict corner $x=1$ is $p(1)g(\theta)$ and
it is (strictly) decreasing in truthfulness.  In particular

$$x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},$$

the lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser for every interior
type and the truthful type $\theta =1$ is indifferent.  In the usual
decreasing–differences language $C_{\theta x}<0$ on the support and the
optimal audit quality is weakly increasing in $\theta$: a higher $\theta$
makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.  In the strict monotone
sense

$$x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\;\;\hbox{for }\;\theta'>\theta $$

never occurs in the interior.  Formally the strict monotone set is
empty; up to the degenerate indifference at the top the weak
preference for the lenient corner is $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $\theta<1$, and
on the canonical two–point support $\{0,1\}$ this is the strict
preference $x^{*}(0)=0$, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the
malpractice type strictly prefers the lenient auditor and the more
truthful type is never strictly more lenient.  This is the usual
reverse sorting $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, the
cost disadvantage of strictness $ \Delta(\theta)$ falling with
truthfulness and vanishing only at $\theta=1$. ∎

2.text:
Up to the $x$ free term $t(\theta)$ the $x$ dependent part of the expected
payment can be written

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x):=xp(x),
$$

on the interior $0\le\theta<1$, $g(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing
hence

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow 
g(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,
$$

so that $g$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and $g'(\theta)
=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever the derivative exists.  On
the two point lattice

$$
\tilde C(\theta,0)=0,\qquad 
\tilde C(\theta,1)=p_{1}g(\theta),\qquad p_{1}=p(1)>0,
$$

and with the additive $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p_{1}g(\theta)
      =p_{1}(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$
$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad\Delta(\theta)>0\;\;{\rm iff}\;\;\theta<1 .
$$

Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

i.e. apart from the degenerate top type the lenient corner $x=0$ strictly
dominates the strict corner $x=1$ and up to the irrelevant $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate.  In particular

$$
\Delta_{\theta}(\theta)=p_{1}\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

so the gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  The $x$ dependent part has
decreasing differences

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x)<0\quad{\rm if}\;h'(x)>0,
$$

so that with the usual normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ the
single crossing property is

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
   =\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]<0,
   \qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and the optimal $x^{*}$ is
weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The incentive to avoid the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$ is

$$
\pi(x,\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),
$$

which is decreasing in $\theta$ for every $x$ and hence the cost
disadvantage of a strict auditor falls with $\theta$.  On the binary
support $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$ the ranking of the two auditors is
$\theta$-independent up to the strictly decreasing scale $g(\theta)$:
every non-perfect type strictly prefers the lenient auditor and the
perfect type is indifferent.  In the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\qquad{\rm for}\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

never occurs on $(0,1)$; the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and indeterminate at $\theta=1$.
Formally the strict monotone set is empty; weakly the lenient auditor
is optimal for the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$, with the unique
indifference point $\Delta(1)=0$.  On the canonical two type
specification this is the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring
$x=0$ and the truthful type $\theta=1$ indifferent, the usual
statement being the pooling on the lenient corner and the opposite
sorting $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, i.e. a more
truthful firm is weakly more willing to bear strictness.  This is the
decreasing-differences, i.e. $C_{\theta x}<0$, case.  The sign of
$h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not pinned down by $p$ decreasing alone; a strict
move to a more lenient auditor with higher $\theta$ would require
$h'(x)<0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ decreasing in $x$, which is not implied by the
assumptions. ∎

6.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta )$ the expected extra payment which
determines the choice of the auditor is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{{\rm no\;report}\}{\mathbb P}
\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)
        =x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)\,x p(x)
$$

with

$$
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad h(1)=0 .
$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so that on $[0,1)$

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow 
h(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,
$$

i.e. $h$ is strictly decreasing and $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)
+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever it exists.  In particular

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ iff $\theta<1$.  Hence on the
binary lattice

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$
and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  Up to the irrelevant additive $t(\theta)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)h(\theta),\qquad \theta<1,
$$

so that

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

is the unique cost minimiser on the interior.  The gain from leniency is

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta) ,
$$

strictly decreasing in $\theta$ because $h$ is strictly decreasing.
In monotone comparative statics

$$
\Delta_{x}C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big],\qquad
\Delta_{\theta}\Delta_{x}C(\theta ,x)=h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0
$$

on the range where $xp(x)$ is increasing, so $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta ,x)$.  The incremental cost of moving from the
lenient to the strict auditor is

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=\big[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\big]p(1)<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. the cost disadvantage of strictness falls with truthfulness.
On $\{0,1\}$ $0\cdot p(0)=0<1\cdot p(1)$ so $xp(x)$ is increasing and the
usual weak optimum is weakly increasing in $\theta$; the more truthful
the firm the weaker is its incentive to avoid the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$.

In particular the strict preference $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ holds for
every interior type, $0\le\theta<1$, with the conventional strict case
$\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$ and the truthful limit
$\theta=1$ being the indifference point $\Delta(1)=0$.  On the interior
the best response is flat, $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, so that
there is no interior $\theta$ at which a strictly larger $\theta$
strictly induces a strictly smaller $x$.  In the strict monotone sense
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ the set is empty; up to the trivial indifference at
the top the weak pooling set for the lenient auditor is $\theta<1$,
normally phrased as the whole interior $[0,1)$ with the degenerate
indifference $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$.  This is the familiar pooling on the
lenient corner and the reverse sorting, $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$, i.e. the cost disadvantage of a strict auditor
is decreasing in truthfulness. ∎

4.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the firm minimises

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm Prob}\{ {\rm no\;report}\}\;p(x)F(\theta)
               =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)
               =g(\theta )h(x) ,
$$

$$
g(\theta ):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0 ,\qquad h(x):=xp(x) ,
$$

on $0\le \theta\le1$.  $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so that on
$[0,1)$

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})=
(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,\qquad
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

and $g(1)=0$.  In particular $g$ is strictly decreasing, $g'(\theta)
=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$, and

$$
C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)
        =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
$$

and in the monotone sense

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .
$$

Hence on the two point technology $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(\theta ,0)=C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)$ for $\theta=1$.  Up to the
trivial additive term $t(\theta)$ the lenient corner dominates the
strict corner on the whole interior,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),
$$

with indifference $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$ at the top.  The gain from
leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness: the expected penalty
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$, so the incentive to
avoid the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ weakens as $\theta$ rises.  In
formal comparative statics

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x),\qquad g'<0,
$$

so that ${\rm sign}\,C_{\theta x}=-{\rm sign}\,h'(x)$.  With
$h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ the cost is submodular, $C_{\theta x}<0$, iff
$h'>0$, i.e. $x^{*}$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  On the binary
support the ranking is $h(0)<h(1)$ for every $g(\theta)>0$ and the
best response is flat on the interior.

Hence there is no interior $\theta$ at which a strict increase in
truthfulness is accompanied by a strict decrease in the optimal
auditor quality; $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ never occurs in the interior.  In the strict
monotone sense the set of types for which a more truthful firm moves
to a strictly more lenient auditor is empty, the conventional
indifference being $\theta=1$.

In weak terms the lenient auditor is (strictly) preferred for every
imperfectly truthful type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$,
i.e. the weak preference set is $\theta\in[0,1)$.  On the canonical
two–type support $\{\theta=0,\theta=1\}$ this is the familiar pooling
statement $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, the
malpractice type strictly preferring the lenient auditor and the
truthful type being the degenerate indifference point. The usual
decreasing–differences sorting is the opposite one: a higher $\theta$
makes the cost of strictness $\Delta(\theta)$ smaller and the demand for
strictness is weakly increasing with truthfulness. ∎

5.text:
Up to the $x$--free term $t(\theta)$ the expected extra payment which is
relevant for the choice of auditor is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{{\rm no\;report}\}{\mathbb P}\{{\rm
RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)\,x p(x) ,
$$

with

$$
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad 0\le \theta<1,\qquad 
h(1)=0 .
$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing, hence $h$ is strictly decreasing on
$[0,1)$ and $h(1)=0$.  On the two point lattice $x\in\{0,1\}$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,0)=0,\qquad 
\widetilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)h(\theta),
$$

and with the $t(\theta)$ term

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+\widetilde C(\theta ,x),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

so that on the interior the lenient corner strictly dominates the
strict corner

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate, $\Delta(1)=0$.  In particular

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. the cost of moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$,

$$
\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  The cost function has
decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$,

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=h'(\theta)xp(x)<0,
$$

so that in the monotone comparative statics sense $x^{*}(\theta)$ is
weakly increasing in $\theta$: the strict auditor becomes relatively
cheaper as $\theta$ rises.  There is therefore no interior type for
which an increase in $\theta$ is associated with a strict move to a
more lenient auditor.  In the strict monotone sense the downward
sorting set

$$
\{\theta:x^{*}(\theta')>x^{*}(\theta)\;\forall\;\theta'<\theta\}
$$

is empty; up to the trivial indifference at the top $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$
on $[0,1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate.  On the canonical
two–point support this is the familiar pooling on leniency,
$x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. weakly every
non–truthful type, $0\le\theta<1$, and in the discrete $0,1$ case the
malpractice type $\theta=0$, strictly prefers the lenient auditor,
the gain from leniency being $\Delta(\theta)>0$ and vanishing only at
the degenerate limit $\theta\to1$.  This is the usual
$x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing, i.e. “bad drives out good’’,
sorting. ∎

8.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the expected extra payment is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
        =h(\theta )\,h_{2}(x),\qquad 
h(\theta ):=(1-\theta )F(\theta ),\qquad h_{2}(x):=xp(x),
$$

and $h(\theta )>0$ for $\theta<1$, $h(1)=0$, is strictly decreasing on
$[0,1)$ because $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing.  On the two point
lattice

$$
h_{2}(0)=0< h_{2}(1)=p(1) ,
$$

so that, up to $t(\theta )$,

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h_{2}(1)h(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta )F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every $\theta<1$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+p(1)h(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The lenient corner is therefore the unique
strict minimiser on the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

and the gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness with $G(1)=0$.
In particular $C_{\theta x}=h'(\theta)h_{2}'(x)<0$ on the interior,
so that $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and the
textbook monotone comparative static is

$$
{\rm sign}\,C_{\theta x}<0\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
x^{*}(\theta)\ {\rm weakly\ increasing\ in}\ \theta .
$$

With the binary technology $h_{2}$ increasing the cost of moving
$0\to1$ falls with $\theta$ but it is always positive for $\theta<1$,
so the best response is flat on the whole interior,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and it is only at the degenerate
limit $h(1)=0$ that indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ obtains.

In the strict monotone sense there is therefore no interior type for
which a strict increase in $\theta$ is associated with a strict move
$x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$.  Formally the strictly decreasing
set is empty, the weak preference for the lenient auditor is
$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior
and, on the usual $\{0,1\}$ support, $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent.  Up to the trivial indifference at the top this
is the conventional phrasing $x^{*}\equiv0$ for every imperfectly
truthful firm, the monotone prediction being the opposite one,
$x^{*}$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, with the usual indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$.  This is the degenerate pooling on $x=0$ that is
normally reported as the empty strict monotone set, weak pooling
$0\le\theta<1$. ∎

3.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the relevant cost is

$$
G(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)\,x p(x),\qquad 
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,
$$

$h(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$ is decreasing and $F$ is decreasing so that on
$[0,1)$

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
\qquad 
h(\theta_{2})<h(\theta_{1}),\;\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $h$ is strictly decreasing and $h(1)=0$.  Put $k(x)=xp(x)$.
On the admissible two point lattice

$$
k(0)=0<k(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

and with the $t(\theta)$ term removed

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta), \qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)h(\theta) ,
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$
$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $0\le\theta<1$.  Hence on the
interior

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

the lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the strict auditor
$x=1$ and up to the additive $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)=C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta),\; \theta =1,
$$

the $x=1$ type being indifferent at the degenerate limit $h(1)=0$.
The gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  In particular

$$
\Delta_{\theta}\Delta_{x}C(\theta ,x)
   =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0
$$

on the conventional normalisation $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $C(\theta ,x)$
has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and $x^{*}$ is a.s.
weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The cost of moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$
falls with truthfulness, so a higher $\theta$ makes a strict auditor
relatively cheaper.  Hence in the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad\forall\;\theta'<\theta
$$

never occurs in the interior; the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate.
In the usual weak formulation the lenient auditor is the unique cost
minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$, with indifference only at the
top type $h(1)=0$.  On the canonical two type support
$\{\,0,1\,\}$ this is $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent,
i.e. the conventional ``bad drives out good'' pooling on the lenient
corner.  In particular there is no interior $\theta$ at which a
strictly larger $\theta$ induces a strictly more lenient choice; the
model predicts the opposite monotone comparative static, $x^{*}(\theta)$
weakly increasing in $\theta$, the only non-trivial change being the
degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.  Up to that trivial boundary
the weak preference for leniency is $\theta<1$, which in the strict
two point formulation is the malpractice type $\theta=0$. ∎

7.text:
Up to the $x$ free term $t(\theta)$ the relevant cost is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{ {\rm refusal}\}{\mathbb P}\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid
{\rm refusal}\}F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x) ,
$$

$$
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x),
$$

$g$ is the product of two decreasing positive functions so that
$g(1)=0$ and

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\ge 0\;\Longrightarrow\;g(\theta_{2})<g(\theta_{1}),
\qquad g'(\theta)<0\;{\rm on}\;[0,1),
$$

and on the two point lattice

$$
h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1) .
$$

Hence, up to $t(\theta)$,

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=g(\theta)p(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\;\;0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]p(1)<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .
$$

So $C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)$ for
every interior type and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

i.e. the lenient corner is the unique strict cost minimiser on
$[0,1)$ and the truthful type $\theta=1$ is indifferent.  In
decreasing differences notation

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]
 =\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]\le0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

so that with $h(1)>h(0)$ $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and the
best response is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The incremental cost
of strictness $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness, $g'(\theta)<0$, so the cost disadvantage of $x=1$ falls
with $\theta$.  In particular the gain from leniency is positive iff
$g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and it vanishes only at the degenerate
limit $g(1)=0$.

Hence on the binary support the (weak) preference for the lenient
auditor is the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$, strictly
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $ \theta<1$, with indifference at the
top $\theta=1$.  In the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\;\;\forall\;\theta'<\theta,
$$

never occurs in the interior; $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and is
weakly increasing in $\theta$.  In the usual two type description this
is $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly preferred by the malpractice type and
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the familiar pooling on the lenient
auditor with the monotone comparative static $x^{*}$ weakly increasing
in $\theta$, the opposite of a strict move to more leniency as
$\theta$ rises.  The empty strict set is the formal statement of the
flat best response; up to the trivial indifference at $\theta=1$ the
weak preference for leniency is $\theta<1$. ∎

preference for the lenient corner is $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $\theta<1$, and
on the canonical two–point support $\{0,1\}$ this is the strict
preference $x^{*}(0)=0$, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the

public_text.2:
Up to the $x$ free term $t(\theta)$ the $x$ dependent part of the expected
payment can be written

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x):=xp(x),
$$

on the interior $0\le\theta<1$, $g(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing
hence

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow 
g(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,
$$

so that $g$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and $g'(\theta)
=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever the derivative exists.  On
the two point lattice

$$
\tilde C(\theta,0)=0,\qquad 
\tilde C(\theta,1)=p_{1}g(\theta),\qquad p_{1}=p(1)>0,
$$

and with the additive $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p_{1}g(\theta)
      =p_{1}(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$
$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad\Delta(\theta)>0\;\;{\rm iff}\;\;\theta<1 .
$$

Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

i.e. apart from the degenerate top type the lenient corner $x=0$ strictly
dominates the strict corner $x=1$ and up to the irrelevant $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate.  In particular

$$
\Delta_{\theta}(\theta)=p_{1}\big[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\big]<0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

so the gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  The $x$ dependent part has
decreasing differences

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x)<0\quad{\rm if}\;h'(x)>0,
$$

so that with the usual normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ the
single crossing property is

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
   =\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]<0,
   \qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and the optimal $x^{*}$ is
weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The incentive to avoid the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$ is

$$
\pi(x,\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),
$$

which is decreasing in $\theta$ for every $x$ and hence the cost
disadvantage of a strict auditor falls with $\theta$.  On the binary
support $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$ the ranking of the two auditors is
$\theta$-independent up to the strictly decreasing scale $g(\theta)$:
every non-perfect type strictly prefers the lenient auditor and the
perfect type is indifferent.  In the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\qquad{\rm for}\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}
$$

never occurs on $(0,1)$; the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and indeterminate at $\theta=1$.
Formally the strict monotone set is empty; weakly the lenient auditor
is optimal for the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$, with the unique
indifference point $\Delta(1)=0$.  On the canonical two type
specification this is the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring
$x=0$ and the truthful type $\theta=1$ indifferent, the usual
statement being the pooling on the lenient corner and the opposite
sorting $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, i.e. a more
truthful firm is weakly more willing to bear strictness.  This is the
decreasing-differences, i.e. $C_{\theta x}<0$, case.  The sign of
$h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not pinned down by $p$ decreasing alone; a strict
move to a more lenient auditor with higher $\theta$ would require
$h'(x)<0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ decreasing in $x$, which is not implied by the
assumptions. ∎

determines the choice of the auditor is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{{\rm no\;report}\}{\mathbb P}

        =x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)\,x p(x)
$$

with

$$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)h(\theta),\qquad \theta<1,

so that

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

is the unique cost minimiser on the interior.  The gain from leniency is

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta) ,
$$

strictly decreasing in $\theta$ because $h$ is strictly decreasing.
In monotone comparative statics

$$
\Delta_{x}C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big],\qquad
\Delta_{\theta}\Delta_{x}C(\theta ,x)=h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0
$$

on the range where $xp(x)$ is increasing, so $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta ,x)$.  The incremental cost of moving from the
lenient to the strict auditor is

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=\big[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\big]p(1)<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. the cost disadvantage of strictness falls with truthfulness.
On $\{0,1\}$ $0\cdot p(0)=0<1\cdot p(1)$ so $xp(x)$ is increasing and the
usual weak optimum is weakly increasing in $\theta$; the more truthful
the firm the weaker is its incentive to avoid the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$.

In particular the strict preference $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ holds for
every interior type, $0\le\theta<1$, with the conventional strict case
$\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$ and the truthful limit
$\theta=1$ being the indifference point $\Delta(1)=0$.  On the interior
the best response is flat, $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, so that
there is no interior $\theta$ at which a strictly larger $\theta$
strictly induces a strictly smaller $x$.  In the strict monotone sense
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ the set is empty; up to the trivial indifference at
the top the weak pooling set for the lenient auditor is $\theta<1$,
normally phrased as the whole interior $[0,1)$ with the degenerate
indifference $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$.  This is the familiar pooling on the
lenient corner and the reverse sorting, $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$, i.e. the cost disadvantage of a strict auditor
is decreasing in truthfulness. ∎
public_text.4:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the firm minimises

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm Prob}\{ {\rm no\;report}\}\;p(x)F(\theta)
               =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)
               =g(\theta )h(x) ,
$$

$$
g(\theta ):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0 ,\qquad h(x):=xp(x) ,
$$

on $0\le \theta\le1$.  $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so that on
$[0,1)$

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})=
(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,\qquad
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

and $g(1)=0$.  In particular $g$ is strictly decreasing, $g'(\theta)
=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$, and

$$
C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)
        =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad \Delta(1)=0,
$$

and in the monotone sense

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .
$$

Hence on the two point technology $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(\theta ,0)=C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)$ for $\theta=1$.  Up to the
trivial additive term $t(\theta)$ the lenient corner dominates the
strict corner on the whole interior,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),
$$

with indifference $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$ at the top.  The gain from
leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness: the expected penalty
$x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$, so the incentive to
avoid the refusal risk $x(1-\theta)$ weakens as $\theta$ rises.  In
formal comparative statics

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x),\qquad g'<0,
$$

so that ${\rm sign}\,C_{\theta x}=-{\rm sign}\,h'(x)$.  With
$h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ the cost is submodular, $C_{\theta x}<0$, iff
$h'>0$, i.e. $x^{*}$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  On the binary
support the ranking is $h(0)<h(1)$ for every $g(\theta)>0$ and the
best response is flat on the interior.

Hence there is no interior $\theta$ at which a strict increase in
truthfulness is accompanied by a strict decrease in the optimal
auditor quality; $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ never occurs in the interior.  In the strict
monotone sense the set of types for which a more truthful firm moves
to a strictly more lenient auditor is empty, the conventional
indifference being $\theta=1$.

In weak terms the lenient auditor is (strictly) preferred for every
imperfectly truthful type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$,
i.e. the weak preference set is $\theta\in[0,1)$.  On the canonical
two–type support $\{\theta=0,\theta=1\}$ this is the familiar pooling
statement $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly, $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, the
malpractice type strictly preferring the lenient auditor and the
truthful type being the degenerate indifference point. The usual
decreasing–differences sorting is the opposite one: a higher $\theta$
makes the cost of strictness $\Delta(\theta)$ smaller and the demand for
strictness is weakly increasing with truthfulness. ∎

Up to the $x$--free term $t(\theta)$ the expected extra payment which is
relevant for the choice of auditor is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{{\rm no\;report}\}{\mathbb P}\{{\rm
RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)\,x p(x) ,
$$

with

$$
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad 0\le \theta<1,\qquad 
h(1)=0 .
$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing, hence $h$ is strictly decreasing on
$[0,1)$ and $h(1)=0$.  On the two point lattice $x\in\{0,1\}$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,0)=0,\qquad 
\widetilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)h(\theta),
$$

and with the $t(\theta)$ term

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+\widetilde C(\theta ,x),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

so that on the interior the lenient corner strictly dominates the
strict corner

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate, $\Delta(1)=0$.  In particular

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta,
$$

i.e. the cost of moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$,

$$
\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  The cost function has
decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$,

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=h'(\theta)xp(x)<0,
$$

so that in the monotone comparative statics sense $x^{*}(\theta)$ is
weakly increasing in $\theta$: the strict auditor becomes relatively
cheaper as $\theta$ rises.  There is therefore no interior type for
which an increase in $\theta$ is associated with a strict move to a
more lenient auditor.  In the strict monotone sense the downward
sorting set

$$
\{\theta:x^{*}(\theta')>x^{*}(\theta)\;\forall\;\theta'<\theta\}
$$

is empty; up to the trivial indifference at the top $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$
on $[0,1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate.  On the canonical
two–point support this is the familiar pooling on leniency,
$x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. weakly every
non–truthful type, $0\le\theta<1$, and in the discrete $0,1$ case the
malpractice type $\theta=0$, strictly prefers the lenient auditor,
the gain from leniency being $\Delta(\theta)>0$ and vanishing only at
the degenerate limit $\theta\to1$.  This is the usual
$x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing, i.e. “bad drives out good’’,
sorting. ∎

Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the expected extra payment is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
        =h(\theta )\,h_{2}(x),\qquad 
h(\theta ):=(1-\theta )F(\theta ),\qquad h_{2}(x):=xp(x),
$$

and $h(\theta )>0$ for $\theta<1$, $h(1)=0$, is strictly decreasing on
$[0,1)$ because $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing.  On the two point
lattice

$$
h_{2}(0)=0< h_{2}(1)=p(1) ,
$$

so that, up to $t(\theta )$,

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h_{2}(1)h(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta )F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every $\theta<1$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+p(1)h(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The lenient corner is therefore the unique
strict minimiser on the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

and the gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness with $G(1)=0$.
In particular $C_{\theta x}=h'(\theta)h_{2}'(x)<0$ on the interior,
so that $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and the
textbook monotone comparative static is

$$
{\rm sign}\,C_{\theta x}<0\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
x^{*}(\theta)\ {\rm weakly\ increasing\ in}\ \theta .
$$

With the binary technology $h_{2}$ increasing the cost of moving
$0\to1$ falls with $\theta$ but it is always positive for $\theta<1$,
so the best response is flat on the whole interior,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and it is only at the degenerate
limit $h(1)=0$ that indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ obtains.

In the strict monotone sense there is therefore no interior type for
which a strict increase in $\theta$ is associated with a strict move
$x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$.  Formally the strictly decreasing
set is empty, the weak preference for the lenient auditor is
$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$ on the interior
and, on the usual $\{0,1\}$ support, $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent.  Up to the trivial indifference at the top this
is the conventional phrasing $x^{*}\equiv0$ for every imperfectly
truthful firm, the monotone prediction being the opposite one,
$x^{*}$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, with the usual indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$.  This is the degenerate pooling on $x=0$ that is
normally reported as the empty strict monotone set, weak pooling
$0\le\theta<1$. ∎
public_text.3:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the relevant cost is

$$
G(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)\,x p(x),\qquad 
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,
$$

$h(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$ is decreasing and $F$ is decreasing so that on
$[0,1)$

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
\qquad 
h(\theta_{2})<h(\theta_{1}),\;\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $h$ is strictly decreasing and $h(1)=0$.  Put $k(x)=xp(x)$.
On the admissible two point lattice

$$
k(0)=0<k(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

and with the $t(\theta)$ term removed

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta), \qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)h(\theta) ,
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$
$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $0\le\theta<1$.  Hence on the
interior

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

the lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the strict auditor
$x=1$ and up to the additive $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(\theta ,0)=C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta),\; \theta =1,
$$

the $x=1$ type being indifferent at the degenerate limit $h(1)=0$.
The gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  In particular

$$
\Delta_{\theta}\Delta_{x}C(\theta ,x)
   =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0
$$

on the conventional normalisation $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $C(\theta ,x)$
has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and $x^{*}$ is a.s.
weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The cost of moving from $x=0$ to $x=1$
falls with truthfulness, so a higher $\theta$ makes a strict auditor
relatively cheaper.  Hence in the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad\forall\;\theta'<\theta
$$

never occurs in the interior; the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and $x^{*}(1)$ is indeterminate.
In the usual weak formulation the lenient auditor is the unique cost
minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$, with indifference only at the
top type $h(1)=0$.  On the canonical two type support
$\{\,0,1\,\}$ this is $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent,
i.e. the conventional ``bad drives out good'' pooling on the lenient
corner.  In particular there is no interior $\theta$ at which a
strictly larger $\theta$ induces a strictly more lenient choice; the
model predicts the opposite monotone comparative static, $x^{*}(\theta)$
weakly increasing in $\theta$, the only non-trivial change being the
degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.  Up to that trivial boundary
the weak preference for leniency is $\theta<1$, which in the strict
two point formulation is the malpractice type $\theta=0$. ∎
public_text.7:
Up to the $x$ free term $t(\theta)$ the relevant cost is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{ {\rm refusal}\}{\mathbb P}\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid
{\rm refusal}\}F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x) ,
$$

$$
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x),
$$

$g$ is the product of two decreasing positive functions so that
$g(1)=0$ and

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\ge 0\;\Longrightarrow\;g(\theta_{2})<g(\theta_{1}),
\qquad g'(\theta)<0\;{\rm on}\;[0,1),
$$

and on the two point lattice

$$
h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1) .
$$

Hence, up to $t(\theta)$,

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=g(\theta)p(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\;\;0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]p(1)<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .
$$

So $C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta ,1)$ for
every interior type and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

i.e. the lenient corner is the unique strict cost minimiser on
$[0,1)$ and the truthful type $\theta=1$ is indifferent.  In
decreasing differences notation

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]
 =\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]\le0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

so that with $h(1)>h(0)$ $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and the
best response is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The incremental cost
of strictness $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
truthfulness, $g'(\theta)<0$, so the cost disadvantage of $x=1$ falls
with $\theta$.  In particular the gain from leniency is positive iff
$g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$ and it vanishes only at the degenerate
limit $g(1)=0$.

Hence on the binary support the (weak) preference for the lenient
auditor is the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$, strictly
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $ \theta<1$, with indifference at the
top $\theta=1$.  In the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\;\;\forall\;\theta'<\theta,
$$

never occurs in the interior; $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and is
weakly increasing in $\theta$.  In the usual two type description this
is $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly preferred by the malpractice type and
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the familiar pooling on the lenient
auditor with the monotone comparative static $x^{*}$ weakly increasing
in $\theta$, the opposite of a strict move to more leniency as
$\theta$ rises.  The empty strict set is the formal statement of the
flat best response; up to the trivial indifference at $\theta=1$ the
weak preference for leniency is $\theta<1$. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ can be dropped. Up to $t$,

$C(\theta,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)xp(x)$,
$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ on $[0,1)$, $h(1)=0$,

$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever it exists, so $h$ is strictly
decreasing. With $h(x)=xp(x)$,

$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)h(x)$,
$C_{\theta x}=h'(\theta)h'(x)$,
so for the usual normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ we have $C_{\theta x}<0$,
i.e. decreasing differences / submodularity in $(\theta,x)$.

On the two-point lattice $x\in\{0,1\}$

$h(0)=0$, $h(1)=p_{1}=p(1)>0$,

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p_{1}h(\theta)
      =p_{1}(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(1)=0$, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,

$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p_{1}\,[h(\theta')-h(\theta)]<0$ for $\theta'>\theta$
on $[0,1)$.

Hence

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+p_{1}h(\theta)=C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$,
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.

The $x$-dependent cost is $g(\theta)h(x)$ with $g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$
strictly decreasing, so the incremental cost of strictness falls with
truthfulness. The unique strict minimiser on the interior is the lenient
corner

$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate; i.e. every
non-perfect type strictly prefers the lenient auditor and the perfect type
is indifferent.

In monotone comparative-statics terms the best response is flat on the
interior, $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, and the textbook monotone
direction is $x^{*}$ weakly increasing in $\theta$: a higher $\theta$ makes a
strict auditor relatively cheaper, the gain from leniency
$G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p_{1}(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ and vanishes only at $\theta=1$.

Strict monotone move to a more lenient auditor, $x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$
for $\theta'>\theta$, never occurs in the interior. Formally the strict
decreasing set is empty; the weak preference for leniency over strictness is
$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, on the canonical binary support
$\{0,1\}$ the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly prefers $x=0$ and the
truthful type $\theta=1$ is the degenerate indifference point.

The sign of $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not pinned down by $p$ decreasing alone and
the implicit function theorem does not apply because $t,p,F$ are only monotone,
not necessarily differentiable, but on the binary technology the ranking is
unambiguous: $h(0)<h(1)$ for every $h(\theta)>0$. The earlier claim of a
weakly decreasing optimal audit with $\theta$ is reversed; the consensus in
this round is the decreasing-differences / $x^{*}$ weakly increasing case with
pooling on the lenient corner and the empty strict monotone set, the weak
pooling set being $\theta<1$, i.e. in the two-type model the low type
$\theta=0$.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The cost up to the x-free term is
$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)xp(x)$ with
$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ on $[0,1)$ and $h(1)=0$.
$1-\theta$ and $F$ decreasing $\Rightarrow$ $h$ strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$,
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever differentiable, and
$h(\theta_{2})<h(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.

On the binary lattice $x\in\{0,1\}$

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$, $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,
$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,
$\Delta(1)=0$, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.
Hence $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every interior type and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.
Up to $t(\theta)$ the lenient corner strictly dominates on $0\le\theta<1$,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with indifference only at $\theta=1$.
The gain from leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ because $h$ is decreasing.

In monotone comparative statics
$C_{\theta x}=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ and $h'<0$.  With the normalisation
$p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ increasing, $C$ has decreasing differences,
$C_{\theta x}<0$, so the (weak) optimal $x^{*}$ is weakly increasing in
$\theta$: a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.
The incremental cost of strictness is decreasing in $\theta$.

Strict monotone movement to a more lenient auditor as $\theta$ rises never
occurs in the interior. The strict preference set for leniency is
$\{\theta<1\}$ with the unique minimiser $x^{*}=0$ for all $\theta<1$ and
indifference at $\theta=1$. On the canonical two-point support this is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$ and the truthful type
$\theta=1$ indifferent. The strict monotone set $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty;
the weak pooling set is $[0,1)$, commonly phrased as $\theta<1$, with the
degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.

The sign of $p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not pinned down by $p$ decreasing alone and
differentiability is not assumed, so the implicit function theorem cannot be
invoked. The disagreement among colleagues is purely terminological about
“decreasing vs increasing’’ sorting; the economically relevant content is
$h$ decreasing so the cost disadvantage of strictness falls with
truthfulness and the model predicts pooling on the lenient auditor for all
imperfectly truthful types, with indifference at the top. The strict
downward sorting set is empty.

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,
$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

Hence $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for every $0\le\theta<1$ and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. The gain from leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ falls with truthfulness and vanishes only at $\theta=1$.

Weakly the lenient auditor is optimal for the whole interior $0\le\theta<1$, in the canonical two-point support $\{0,1\}$ the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly prefers $x=0$ and the truthful type $\theta=1$ is indifferent. $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,
$\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,
$\Delta(1)=0$, $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.

Hence $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every interior type and 
$x^{*}(\theta)=0$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate. 
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $\theta<1$.

$\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ because $h$ is strictly decreasing. The gain from leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ falls with truthfulness. 
$C_{\theta x}=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ iff $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$.
With the usual normalisation $xp(x)$ increasing, $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$: a higher $\theta$ makes a strict auditor relatively cheaper.

On the binary support the ranking of auditors is $\theta$-independent up to the strictly decreasing scale $h(\theta)>0$. The optimal choice is flat, $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, with the only change the degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the top type. 

Strict monotone move $x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$ for $\theta'>\theta$ never occurs in the interior. Formally the strict decreasing set is empty; the weak set where the lenient auditor is weakly optimal is $\theta<1$, with strict preference $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$ and indifference only at $\theta=1$. On the canonical $\{0,1\}$ support this is $\theta=0$ strictly prefers $x=0$ and $\theta=1$ indifferent.

Disagreement in the round is verbal: Colleagues 2,4 state “optimal audit quality is (weakly) decreasing in $\theta$” while the decreasing-differences calculation gives $x^{*}$ weakly increasing. The pointwise optimum is the same: pooling on $x=0$ for all $\theta<1$. The sign of $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not pinned down by $p$ decreasing alone; for the binary case $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$ is enough for the pooling result. No interior $\theta$ induces a strict move to a more lenient auditor as $\theta$ rises; the model predicts the opposite comparative static, i.e. the cost disadvantage of strictness falls with truthfulness. ∎

8.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the part of the expected payment which is
relevant for the choice of $x$ is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{ {\rm no\;report}\}\,
 {\mathbb P}\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)
       =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)h_{2}(x) ,
$$

$$
h(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(1)=0,\qquad 
h_{2}(x):=xp(x),
$$

and with $1-\theta\downarrow$, $F\downarrow$

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0\qquad0\le\theta<1 ,
$$

so that $h$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and $h(1)=0$.  With

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=h'(\theta)h_{2}'(x),
$$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,0)=0,\qquad 
\widetilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)h(\theta),
$$
so that, up to $t(\theta)$,

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)
      =p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$
$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
$$
and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\big[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\big]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta ,
$$

i.e. the incremental cost of moving from the lenient corner to the
strict corner is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and it vanishes
only at the degenerate limit $h(1)=0$.  Hence on $\{0,1\}$

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+p(1)h(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  In particular

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

is the unique strict minimiser on the interior and
$x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$ is indeterminate, $\Delta(1)=0$.  The gain from

so that $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta,x)$ and the
textbook monotone comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$: a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor
relatively cheaper.  On the binary technology the best response is
flat on the whole interior,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0\ \hbox{on }[0,1),\qquad x^{*}(1)\ \hbox{indifferent},

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad{\rm for}\;\theta'>\theta
$$

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff h(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
$$

6.text:

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm P}\{ {\rm refusal}\}{\rm P}\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid

      =g(\theta)h(x),\qquad
g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta),\;\;h(x):=xp(x),

$g(\theta)>0$ on $[0,1),\;g(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing, so

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})=(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})

i.e. $g$ is strictly decreasing and $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)

      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes only at the
degenerate limit $g(1)=0$.  Hence, up to the irrelevant additive

$$

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
  =\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[h(x')-h(x)\bigr]\le0,

increasing in $\theta$.  The cost disadvantage of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$, i.e. a more truthful firm is
relatively less averse to strictness.

In particular the best response is flat on the whole interior,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, so that in the strict monotone
sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad{\rm for}\quad \theta'>\theta
$$

canonical two–type support this is the familiar pooling

i.e. $x^{*}$ is weakly increasing, not decreasing, in $\theta$.  The
empty strict set is the formal expression of the flat best response
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with the degenerate indifference

strict minimiser for every imperfectly truthful type, $C(\theta,0)<
C(\theta,1)\Leftrightarrow\theta<1$, with indifference only at

2.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax the $x$ dependent part of the expected payment is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm Prob}\{ {\rm refusal}\}\;{\rm Prob}\{{\rm RS}|{\rm refusal}\}
F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x)
$$

with

$$
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad 0\le \theta<1,\qquad g(1)=0,
\qquad h(x)=xp(x),
$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ being decreasing so that on $[0,1)$

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})=(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,

i.e. $g$ is strictly decreasing and $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x),
$$
