differences in $(\theta ,x)$.

On the admissible binary technology

$$
h(0)=0,\qquad h(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),
$$

and up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .
$$

Hence for every interior type the incremental cost of moving from the
lenient corner to the strict corner is strictly positive and strictly
decreasing in truthfulness,

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+p_{1}g(\theta)=C(\theta,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

is the unique strict cost minimiser on the interior.  The gain from
leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)=p_{1}h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishes only at the degenerate
limit $h(1)=0$.  In monotone comparative statics

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
   =\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[h(x')-h(x)\bigr]\le0,
   \qquad \theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and the best response is weakly
increasing in $\theta$: the cost disadvantage of a strict auditor,
$\Delta(\theta)$, falls with $\theta$, so a higher $\theta$ makes the
strict auditor relatively cheaper.

In particular there is no interior type for which a strict increase in
truthfulness is accompanied by a strict decrease in the optimal auditor
quality.  On the interior the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, and

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\qquad {\rm for}\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs.  Formally the strict monotone decreasing set is empty.
Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser iff
$g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $\theta<1$, with indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the
top.  On the canonical two–type support $\{\theta=0,\theta=1\}$ this is
the familiar pooling on the lenient corner,
$x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, the malpractice type
strictly preferring the lenient auditor and the more truthful type being
never strictly more lenient.  This is the usual $x^{*}$ weakly increasing
in $\theta$ sorting, the opposite of a strict move to more leniency as
$\theta$ rises. ∎

3.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax $t(\theta)$ the $x$ part of the expected payment is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),\qquad
g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta),\;h(x):=xp(x),
$$

$g(1)=0$, $g(\theta)>0$ for $0\le \theta<1$ and $1-\theta$ and $F$ decreasing
gives $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$, i.e. $g$ is strictly
decreasing on $[0,1)$ and $g(1)=0$.  On the two point technology

$$
h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

so that with $C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+\widetilde C(\theta ,x)$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $0\le\theta<1$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

and up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta,0)=0<\widetilde C(\theta,1)=p(1)g(\theta),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

i.e.

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

the lenient corner is the unique strict minimiser on the interior and
the truthful type is indifferent, $\Delta(1)=0$.  The gain from
leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness,
$\Delta_{\theta}(\theta)=p(1)g'(\theta)<0$ on $[0,1)$, so that the
incremental cost of moving $0\to1$ falls with $\theta$.

In particular

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x)<0,\qquad h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0,
$$

so $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$.  With $h(0)<h(1)$
the single-crossing property gives
$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0$ for
$\theta'>\theta$, i.e. the best response is a.s. weakly increasing in
$\theta$: a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.
On the binary support the ranking of the two auditors is $\theta$-
independent up to the strictly decreasing scale $g(\theta)>0$ and the
best response is flat,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0\;\hbox{on}\;[0,1),
$$

so that in the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\;\;\hbox{for}\;\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs in the interior.  Formally the strictly decreasing set is
empty.  In weak terms the lenient auditor is strictly preferred for
every imperfectly truthful type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$,
with the degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the top.  On the
canonical two-type support this is $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, the usual pooling on $x=0$ for all $\theta<1$
and the opposite sorting $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in
$\theta$.  This is the claimed flat, essentially $x^{*}\equiv0$,
best response; the only non-trivial change is the indifference at
$\theta=1$. ∎

7.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax $t(\theta)$ the $x$ dependent part of the expected
payment is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
        =g(\theta )h(x),\qquad 
g(\theta ):=(1-\theta )F(\theta ),\;\;h(x):=xp(x),
$$

$g(1)=0$, $g(\theta)>0$ on $[0,1)$ and $1-\theta ,F$ decreasing give

$$
g(\theta_{2})<g(\theta_{1})\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\ge 0,
\qquad g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
$$

so that $g$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,1)$ and
$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x)$ has
$C_{\theta x}=g'(\theta)h'(x)$.  On the admissible binary lattice

$$
h(0)=0,\qquad h(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,0)=0,\qquad 
\widetilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)g(\theta),
$$

and with the additive $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$
$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
$$
$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta .
$$

Hence on the interior

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  Up to $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate, i.e. the lenient corner strictly
dominates the strict corner for every imperfectly truthful type and the
perfect type is the degenerate indifference point $\Delta(1)=0$.
The gain from leniency
$G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing
in $\theta$ and

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-\big[C(\theta,x')-C(\theta,x)\big]
  =\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]\big[h(x')-h(x)\big]\le0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta ,\;x'>x,
$$

so that $C$ is sub-modular in $(\theta ,x)$ and on the normalisation
$h'(x)>0$ the usual monotone comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$
weakly increasing in $\theta$.  In particular the cost of moving
$0\to1$ falls with $\theta$ and

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad{\rm for}\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs in the interior.  The best response is flat
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and indeterminate at $\theta=1$; in the
strict monotone sense the decreasing set is empty.  In weak terms
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ iff $g(\theta)>0$ iff $\theta<1$,
i.e. leniency is the unique strict minimiser for every
$0\le\theta<1$ and on the canonical two point support $\{0,1\}$ this is
the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$ with the
truthful type $\theta=1$ indifferent, $\Delta(1)=0$.  This is the
conventional pooling on the lenient corner and the reverse sorting
$x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$, the usual statement being
the empty strict monotone decreasing set, up to the trivial
indifference at the top. ∎

4.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the $x$-dependent part of the expected
payment is

$$\tilde C(\theta ,x)={\rm Prob}\{no\,report\}p(x)F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x), $$
$$g(\theta):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x):=xp(x),$$
$g(1)=0$.  $1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing, hence on $[0,1)$

$$g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})=(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-
(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},$$
and $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$.  With $C(\theta ,x)=
t(\theta)+\tilde C(\theta ,x)$

$$C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x),\qquad 
C(\theta',x)-C(\theta',x')-C(\theta,x)+C(\theta,x')
 =\big[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\big]\big[h(x)-h(x')\big] .$$

On the binary technology $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$ and

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(1)g(\theta)
        =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,$$
$$\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
$$
$$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,$$

i.e. the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor is strictly decreasing
in $\theta$ and vanishes only at the top.  Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$\tilde C(\theta ,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad0\le\theta<1,$$
$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1),\qquad 
0\le\theta<1,$$
$$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),$$

so that

$$x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},$$

the lenient corner is the unique strict minimiser on the interior.
In particular the gain from leniency

$$G(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness.  With the conventional
normalisation $h'(x)>0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ increasing, $C$ has decreasing
differences in $(\theta,x)$ and $C_{\theta x}<0$; the usual monotone
comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$.
The cost of moving $0\to1$ falls with $\theta$, so a higher $\theta$
makes strictness relatively cheaper.

In the strict monotone sense $x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$ for
$\theta'>\theta$ never occurs on the interior: the best response is
flat, $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, with the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the top.  The strictly decreasing set

$$\{\theta:dx^{*}/d\theta<0\}$$

is therefore empty.  Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique cost
minimiser iff $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$,
with indifference at $\theta=1$.  On the canonical two point support
$\{0,1\}$ this is the familiar pooling $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. every imperfectly truthful type pools on
the lenient corner and the monotone prediction is $x^{*}$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$, the opposite of a strict move to more leniency
as $\theta$ rises.  This is the stated empty strict monotone set, the
weak pooling set being $0\le\theta<1$, normally quoted as the malpractice
type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$. ∎

1.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the relevant part of the expected
payment is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)={\mathbb P}\{{\rm no\;report}\}{\mathbb P}\{{\rm RS}\mid
{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)
      =g(\theta)h(x),
$$

$$
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x), \qquad 
g(1)=0 .
$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so that on $[0,1)$

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})
   =(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,
\qquad \theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ wherever it exists
and $g$ is strictly decreasing with $g(1)=0$.  On the admissible
two point lattice

$$
h(0)=0,\qquad h(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

and with the additive $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

Hence

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta ,
$$

so that the incremental cost of moving $0\to1$

$$
G(\theta)=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes only at the
degenerate limit $g(1)=0$.  Up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad 
0\le\theta<1,
$$

i.e.

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

and in the binary model

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

the lenient corner is the unique strict minimiser on the whole
interior and the perfect type $\theta=1$ is the degenerate indifference
point $\Delta(1)=0$.

In particular

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x),\qquad g'<0,
$$

so that on the conventional normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$,
i.e. $xp(x)$ increasing, $C$ has decreasing differences in
$(\theta ,x)$,

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
   =\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[h(x')-h(x)\bigr]<0,
   \qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

and the usual monotone comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$.  The cost disadvantage of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$, so a higher
$\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

Hence in the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad{\rm for}\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs on $(0,1)$; the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, with the trivial indifference at the
top.  Formally the strictly decreasing best-response set is empty.
Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique cost minimiser for every
imperfectly truthful type, $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$, i.e.
the weak pooling set for leniency is $0\le\theta<1$ and on the canonical
$\{0,1\}$ support this is $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent,
the usual ``bad drives out good’’ pooling on $x=0$.  This is the
opposite of a strict move to more leniency as truthfulness rises. ∎

$$

 {\mathbb P}\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta)

increasing in $\theta$: a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor
relatively cheaper.  On the binary technology the best response is

$$

empty.  Weakly the lenient auditor strictly dominates the strict
auditor for every imperfectly truthful type,

$$

$$

i.e. up to the degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ the pooling
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $0\le\theta<1$.  On the canonical two-type support

where it exists.  With the additive term $t(\theta)$

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x),\qquad 
C_{\theta x}(\theta ,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x),
$$

so that on the range where $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ the cost has decreasing
differences in $(\theta ,x)$.

On the admissible binary technology

$$
h(0)=0,\qquad h(1)=p(1)>0,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),
$$

and up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .
$$

Hence for every interior type the incremental cost of moving from the
lenient corner to the strict corner is strictly positive and strictly
decreasing in truthfulness,

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+p_{1}g(\theta)=C(\theta,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

so that up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

is the unique strict cost minimiser on the interior.  The gain from
leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)=p_{1}h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishes only at the degenerate
limit $h(1)=0$.  In monotone comparative statics

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
   =\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[h(x')-h(x)\bigr]\le0,
   \qquad \theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and the best response is weakly
increasing in $\theta$: the cost disadvantage of a strict auditor,
$\Delta(\theta)$, falls with $\theta$, so a higher $\theta$ makes the
strict auditor relatively cheaper.

In particular there is no interior type for which a strict increase in
truthfulness is accompanied by a strict decrease in the optimal auditor
quality.  On the interior the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, and

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\qquad {\rm for}\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs.  Formally the strict monotone decreasing set is empty.
Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser iff
$g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $\theta<1$, with indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the
top.  On the canonical two–type support $\{\theta=0,\theta=1\}$ this is
the familiar pooling on the lenient corner,
$x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, the malpractice type
strictly preferring the lenient auditor and the more truthful type being
never strictly more lenient.  This is the usual $x^{*}$ weakly increasing
in $\theta$ sorting, the opposite of a strict move to more leniency as
$\theta$ rises. ∎

and $g(\theta_{2})<g(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.
$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x)$,
$C_{\theta x}=g'(\theta)h'(x)$.

On the binary technology $h(0)=0$, $h(1)=p(1)>0$,

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta)$,

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(1)=0$, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,

$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0$ for
$\theta'>\theta$.

Hence on the interior $\tilde C(\theta,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta,1)$,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$ and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.
The unique strict minimiser is

$x^{*}(\theta)=0$, $0\le\theta<1$, $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate,

the lenient corner strictly dominates the strict corner.

Gain from leniency $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is
strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishes only at $g(1)=0$.
Decreasing differences

$C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
=[g(\theta')-g(\theta)][h(x')-h(x)]\le0$
for $\theta'>\theta$, $x'>x$,

so with the conventional normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$,
$C_{\theta x}<0$ and the textbook monotone comparative static is
$x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$: the incremental cost of
$0\to1$ falls with $\theta$, a higher $\theta$ makes a strict auditor
relatively cheaper.

There is no interior type at which a strict increase in $\theta$ induces
a strict decrease in $x^{*}$. The strict monotone decreasing best-response
set $\{\theta:x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\ \forall\theta'<\theta\}$ is
empty; the best response is flat $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with the
degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the top.

i.e. $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$. On the canonical
$\{0,1\}$ support this is $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent.

The sign of $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)$ is not identified by $p$ decreasing alone
in the continuum; on the binary lattice $h(0)<h(1)$ is guaranteed and the
pooling result holds. Earlier confusion about $x^{*}$ decreasing in $\theta$
is resolved: $g$ decreasing makes strictness relatively cheaper as $\theta$
rises, the opposite of “bad drives out good”. Consensus in round 2 is
pooling on $x=0$ for all imperfect types, empty strict decreasing set,
weak pooling set $\theta<1$ with indifference at $\theta=1$. ∎

$$

=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 .

\qquad\theta'>\theta,

so the incremental cost of strictness $G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ is

$$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)

2.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the $x$-dependent expected payment is

$$\widetilde C(\theta ,x)={\mathbb P}\{no\;report\}{\mathbb P}\{RS\mid no\;report\}F(\theta)
 =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x) ,
$$

$$g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\;{\rm on}\;[0,1),\;g(1)=0,\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x) ,
$$

and $1-\theta$ and $F$ decreasing gives on $[0,1)$

$$g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})<0\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},\qquad 
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,$$

C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
 =[g(\theta')-g(\theta)][h(x')-h(x)]\le0,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$.  On the binary technology
$h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)>0$,

$$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),$$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 ,$$

$$\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,$$
$$\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0,\qquad
\theta'>\theta .$$

Hence up to $t(\theta)$ the incremental cost of strictness
$G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and
vanishes only at the degenerate limit $g(1)=0$,

$$\widetilde C(\theta,0)=0<\widetilde C(\theta,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad
0\le\theta<1,$$

$$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).$$

On the admissible two point lattice the unique strict minimiser on the
interior is therefore

$$x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$
with $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$ the degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.
In particular the best response is flat on the interior,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$,
and with the conventional normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ the
textbook monotone comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$; the cost disadvantage of a strict auditor
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)g(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$ so a higher $\theta$
makes strictness relatively cheaper.

In the strict monotone sense

$$x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad{\rm for}\ \theta'>\theta$$

never occurs on $(0,1)$.  Formally the strictly decreasing best
response set is empty.  Weakly the lenient corner strictly dominates
the strict corner iff $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff

of a strict move to more leniency as truthfulness rises. ∎

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0\quad{\rm on}\;[0,1),

so that in the strict monotone sense

$$

3.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the $x$-dependent part of the
expected payment is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)= {\mathbb P}\{no\;report\}{\mathbb P}\{RS\mid no\;report\}
F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x) ,
$$

$$
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad h(x)=xp(x),\qquad g(1)=0 .
$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so that on $[0,1)$

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})=(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-
(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0,\qquad \theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $g$ is strictly decreasing with $g(1)=0$, and $C(\theta,x)=
t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x)$.  On the admissible binary technology
$h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),\tag{1}
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
       =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0,
\qquad \theta'>\theta .
$$

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta,0)=0<\widetilde C(\theta,1)=p(1)g(\theta),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

so that on the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

and the gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and $G(1)=0$.  With the
conventional normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$,

$$
C_{\theta x}(\theta,x)=g'(\theta)h'(x)<0,
$$

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
 =\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[h(x')-h(x)\bigr]\le0 ,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and the textbook monotone
comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$.

so a higher $\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

In particular

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad{\rm for}\;\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs on $(0,1)$: the best response is flat,
$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the top.  The strict monotone decreasing best-response
set is empty.  In weak terms the lenient corner strictly dominates the
strict corner iff $g(\theta)>0$, i.e. $C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$,
with indifference at $\theta=1$.  On the canonical two point support

preferred by the malpractice type and $x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, i.e. the
weak preference for leniency is the whole interior $[0,1)$, normally
quoted as the malpractice type $\theta=0$.  This is the usual $x^{*}$

F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),
$$

$$

$$

and $1-\theta\downarrow ,F\downarrow$ gives on $[0,1)$

$$

=(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})<0 ,
\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ where it exists and
$g$ is strictly decreasing with $g(1)=0$.  With $C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)$

$$
C_{\theta x}=g'(\theta)h'(x) ,
$$

so that on the usual normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ the cost has
decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$.

On the binary lattice $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
         =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad\Delta(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta .
$$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,0)=0<\widetilde C(\theta ,1)=p(1)g(\theta),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

and

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

is the unique strict minimiser on the interior.  The gain from leniency

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishes only at $g(1)=0$.
Hence

$$
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
 =\bigl[g(\theta')-g(\theta)\bigr]\bigl[h(x')-h(x)\bigr]\le0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
$$

i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and on $h(1)>h(0)$ the
text-book monotone comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly
increasing in $\theta$: the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor
$\Delta(\theta)$ falls with $\theta$ and the strict auditor becomes
relatively cheaper as truthfulness rises.

In particular the best response is flat on the whole interior,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0\quad{\rm on}\;[0,1),
$$

so that in the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\quad{\rm for}\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs in the interior.  Formally the strictly decreasing
best-response set $\{\theta:dx^{*}/d\theta<0\}$ is empty, with the
degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the top.  Weakly the lenient
corner strictly dominates the strict corner iff $g(\theta)>0$, i.e.

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1,
$$

quoted as the malpractice type $\theta=0$ strictly preferring $x=0$
and the perfect type $\theta=1$ indifferent, $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly and
$x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate.  This is the familiar ``bad drives out good''
pooling on $x=0$ and the opposite of a strict move to more leniency as
$\theta$ rises. ∎

$x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ and indeterminate at the degenerate
indifference $\theta=1$. In the strict monotone sense
$x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)$ for $\theta'>\theta$ never occurs in the
interior; the strictly decreasing best-response set is empty.

Weakly, the lenient auditor is the unique cost minimiser iff

decreasing alone does not imply $xp$ decreasing and the implicit function
theorem does not apply. The binary case is sufficient for the pooling
result: $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$.

Unresolved wording: the weak preference set for leniency is
$\theta<1$ – on the two-type model $\theta=0$ – whereas the strict

interior support. Colleagues consistently report pooling on $x=0$ for
every imperfectly truthful type and the opposite sorting, $x^{*}$
weakly increasing, usually phrased as “bad drives out good”.

2.text:
The $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ can be dropped.  Up to $t$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)={\mathbb P}\{no\,report\}{\mathbb P}\{RS\mid no\,report\}F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),
$$

$$
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0\;{\rm on}\;[0,1),\;g(1)=0,\qquad 
h(x)=xp(x),\qquad C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+g(\theta)h(x) .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ give on $[0,1)$

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})<0\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},\qquad 
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0 ,
$$

so that $g$ is strictly decreasing to $0$ and

$$
C_{\theta x}=g'(\theta)h'(x),\qquad 
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
=[g(\theta')-g(\theta)][h(x')-h(x)]\le0,
$$

i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in $(\theta ,x)$ and on the
conventional normalisation $h'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ it is submodular,
$C_{\theta x}<0$.

On the binary technology $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(1)=0,\qquad \Delta(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1,
\qquad 
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0,
\;\theta'>\theta .
$$

Hence up to $t$

$$
\tilde C(\theta,0)=0<\tilde C(\theta,1)=p(1)g(\theta),\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
$$

In particular the incremental cost of strictness

$$
G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes only at $g(1)=0$.
The unique strict minimiser on the interior is therefore

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the top.  The cost disadvantage of a strict auditor
falls with $\theta$, so with $h(1)>h(0)$ the textbook monotone
comparative static is $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$:
the strict auditor becomes relatively cheaper as truthfulness rises.
In the strict monotone sense

$$
x^{*}(\theta')<x^{*}(\theta)\qquad{\rm for}\;\theta'>\theta
$$

never occurs on the interior.  Formally the strictly decreasing
best-response set is empty, i.e. there is no $\theta'>\theta$ with a
strict move to a more lenient auditor.  The best response is flat,
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  In weak terms the lenient corner strictly
dominates the strict corner iff $g(\theta)>0$, i.e.
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1$, with indifference only at
$\theta=1$.  On the canonical two-point support this is the familiar
pooling $x^{*}(0)=0$ strictly preferred by the malpractice type and
$x^{*}(1)$ indifferent, the usual ``bad drives out good'' $x^{*}$ weakly
increasing sorting.  This is often quoted as the whole imperfectly
truthful set $0\le\theta<1$, in particular the malpractice type
$\theta=0$, strictly preferring the lenient auditor to the strict one.

7.text:
On the $x$ free tax the choice relevant expected payment is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)={\mathbf P}\{no\,report\}{\mathbf P}\{RS\mid no\,report\}
F(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=g(\theta)h(x),
$$

$$
g(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta),\qquad h(x)=xp(x),\qquad 
C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+\widetilde C(\theta,x),
$$

$g(1)=0$, $g(\theta)>0$ on $[0,1)$ and $1-\theta\downarrow$, $F\downarrow$
imply on $[0,1)$

$$
g(\theta_{2})-g(\theta_{1})<0,\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},\qquad 
g'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
$$

so that $g$ is strictly decreasing to $0$.  Hence

$$
C_{\theta x}=g'(\theta)h'(x),\qquad 
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
=[g(\theta')-g(\theta)][h(x')-h(x)]\le 0,
$$

$\theta'>\theta$, $x'>x$, i.e. $C$ has decreasing differences in
$(\theta ,x)$.  On the admissible binary lattice $h(0)=0<h(1)=p(1)$

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+p(1)g(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)g(\theta)
      =p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

$\Delta(1)=0$ and $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff0\le\theta<1$, and

$$
\Delta(\theta')-\Delta(\theta)=p(1)[g(\theta')-g(\theta)]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta ,
$$

so the incremental cost of strictness
$G(\theta)=\Delta(\theta)=p(1)(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing
in truthfulness and $G(1)=0$.  Up to $t$

$$
\widetilde C(\theta,0)=0<\widetilde C(\theta,1)=p(1)g(\theta),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff g(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
$$

Hence on the interior

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,\qquad x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\},
$$

the lenient corner is the unique strict minimiser for every imperfectly
truthful type and the perfect type is the degenerate indifference point
$\Delta(1)=0$.  The best response is flat $x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0$ on

4.text:
